Motors are inductive and draw massive inrush current—known as Locked Rotor Amps (LRA)—during startup. If you size the breaker to the motor's normal running current, it will trip instantly every time you flip the switch. The direct answer: for a standard single-phase AC motor on an inverse-time thermal-magnetic breaker, multiply the motor's Full Load Amps (FLA) by 2.5 (250%) and round up to the next standard breaker size per NEC 240.6.

[web-electricalflux-com-motor-breaker-size-chart-nec-article-430-sizing-.md] (dated 2026) How derating rows modify the base value: Unlike wire ampacity, which requires strict mathematical derating for ambient temperatures above 30°C (86°F) per NEC 310.15, motor branch-circuit short-circuit breakers are not mathematically derated for heat in the same way. The 250% multiplier already provides a massive buffer. However, if your breaker is installed in a high-ambient environment (like an unventilated outdoor pump house in the Southwest hitting 115°F), the breaker's internal thermal bimetallic strip will trip closer to its lower threshold. If you experience 'thermal creep' nuisance tripping in hot environments, the NEC permits you to step up to the next standard breaker size, provided you do not exceed 400% of the FLA for inverse-time breakers under the exceptions in NEC 430.52(C)(1).

[web-kwcalc-com-motor-breaker-size-calculator-nec-motor-protecti.md] (dated 2026) In NEC Article 430, the 125% factor applies to branch-circuit conductors (430.22), and overload relays are set at 115% to 125% of nameplate current (430.32). The branch-circuit breaker is governed by NEC 430.52, which sets a maximum rather than a minimum: up to 250% of the table full-load current for an inverse-time breaker. Sizing the breaker at 125% of FLC, as this calculator does, is a conservative starting point; if it trips during motor starting, it may be increased up to the Table 430.52 limit.

[nec-430.md] (UNDATED: edition not stated) 430.52 and Table 430.52: for a Design B squirrel-cage motor the maximum rating of an inverse-time circuit breaker is 250 percent of the full-load current; for 14 A that is 35 A. The maximum for a nontime-delay fuse is 300 percent (42 A).

[web-kwcalc-com-motor-breaker-size-calculator-nec-motor-protecti.md] (dated 2026) This tool sizes the breaker at 125% of motor full-load current, rounded up to a standard size. NEC 430.52 permits up to 250% of table FLC for inverse-time breakers where needed for starting. Local electrical codes and authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) requirements should always be followed.
